title: Jibu's Failed Water Pilots and the 2014 Restart in Kigali
dek: In 2013 Galen and Randy Welsch's first drinking-water franchises in East Africa all faltered; they rewrote the franchise deal and started again.

story.event: The failure of Jibu's 2013 pilot water franchises and the restart in Kigali and Kampala
story.summary: Galen and Randy Welsch incorporated Jibu in 2012 to franchise drinking-water shops to local entrepreneurs in East Africa. Their self-funded 2013 pilots in Uganda, Rwanda and DR Congo faltered: partners in Rwanda and Congo chased hotel customers instead of ordinary households, and red tape stalled Uganda. Within months they raised money, strengthened the franchise agreement and relaunched in Kigali and Kampala in 2014; by 2021 Jibu had about 150 franchises in seven countries, with Rwanda its most successful market.
paragraphs: In late March 2013, Randy Welsch wrote to Jibu's supporters from the United States, home early from a month in East Africa with his son, Galen. They had gone to open five water businesses, two in Uganda, one in Burundi and two in Congo, and had opened none. Each country lacked at least one item on their launch checklist: equipment still in customs, a shop not ready, a government approval to sell water. He called it their "just kidding" trip.

The Welsches had incorporated Jibu in 2012, Galen just back from the Peace Corps and Randy a retired software executive. The plan: a local owner would run a treatment unit in a busy shopfront, cleaning water from any source and selling it in reusable bottles nearby, at a price meant for ordinary households. Galen later said they had no proven model to show partners "because we hadn't proven it ourselves." So they paid for the pilots themselves and, Randy recalled, ran them in three countries at once, assuming two of the three would fail. In June they dropped Burundi and started from scratch in Rwanda. By late October Galen listed pilots in Kampala, Kigali and Congo, and wrote: "Even if we fail, we believe our efforts will not have been in vain."

Then they did fail. The partners in Rwanda and Congo wanted to sell to hotels, against Coca-Cola's bottled water, rather than to the less well-off households Jibu was built for, and Jibu cut ties with them. In Uganda, red tape stopped full operation. Galen said later that they came closest to giving up "after all three of our pilots failed"; they had expected some failure, he said, not that nothing would work.

Within months they raised outside money, took advice from franchise specialists and strengthened the franchise agreement. In 2014 they relaunched in Kigali and Kampala. That August Galen described price control as part of the agreement, keeping franchises on their target market and "not competing with upper-class water bottlers." One early Kigali reseller, Media Muvuna, had run a small print shop; by 2021 she owned four franchises with 25 staff. That year a Stanford Social Innovation Review podcast counted about 150 franchises in seven countries, Rwanda the most successful; Jibu was not yet profitable overall.

quote.text: And if we come on an impossibility, we give up the search, e.g. if we need money and this cannot be got; but if a thing appears possible we try to do it.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: After three failed pilots, the Welsches faced Aristotle's test: was the thing impossible, or only badly arranged? Safe water at a fair price for ordinary city households still looked possible, and the money to try again could be got. What they changed were the means: the partners, the contract and the customers.

reflection: There is a difference between something that cannot be done and something that has not yet been done well, and in the middle of a bad stretch they feel exactly the same. The Welsches had planned for failure, and it still hit hard when nothing worked. What let them go on was looking at why each pilot had failed. None of the reasons was that city families did not want safe water at a fair price.
When something you have put your energy into falls flat, give yourself a day before deciding what it means. Then ask the plain question: was it the aim that failed, or the arrangement around it?
invitation: Pick one thing that went wrong recently, at work or at home. Write two lines: what you were aiming for, and the one arrangement around it that let you down. Leave the fixing until tomorrow.

cross_checks.claim: Randy and Galen Welsch founded and incorporated Jibu in 2012
Jibu's 2013 pilots were in Uganda, Rwanda (Kigali) and DR Congo
In 2013 the founders planned launches in Burundi but moved the Burundi launch to Rwanda, which entered Jibu's network that year
Jibu's franchise agreement set prices for ordinary households rather than the upmarket bottled-water trade, the issue on which the Rwanda and Congo partners diverged

research_notes: Number of pilots: Galen Welsch's contemporary NextBillion article (dated 31 October 2013 on his NextBillion author page) says four pilots, two in Kampala, one in Kigali and one in DR Congo; Unreasonable (August 2014) says three test stations, one per country; on the SSIR podcast (2021) Randy says three franchises in three countries and Galen says 'all three of our pilots failed'. Randy's 2013 letters planned five launches per trip. The story avoids a count of its own, says pilots ran in three countries, and keeps Galen's 'all three' only inside his quotation. The failure itself rests on the founders' later account in the SSIR episode (narrated by Adeline Sire with Galen and Randy on tape); the contemporary 2013 and 2014 pieces describe the pilots as early-stage or being refined and report no failure, so the story attributes the failure and near-abandonment to Galen. Price control was in the model from the start (NextBillion 2013: a controlled price for the middle 80 per cent of the market), so the story does not claim the 2014 agreement introduced it; it says only that the agreement was strengthened and quotes Galen's August 2014 description. Founders' early money: SSIR says they invested half a million dollars of their own; an uncited 2016 blog (alessandrobenetton.com, not used) says $30,000 in total; the story says only that they paid for the pilots themselves. Franchise fee: $1,000 in 2013-14 (NextBillion, Unreasonable) against a $2,000-3,000 licence fee in 2021 (SSIR); different periods, not used in the story. Media Muvuna: SSIR says both that she bought in 'in 2015' and that she began reselling in 2014 and became a partner four months later, so the story calls her an early reseller and gives only her 2021 position. Jibu's later totals: SSIR (2021) about 150 franchises in seven countries; The New Times (2026) over 200 franchises in eight countries; the story uses the 2021 figure with its date. Wikipedia (not cited) dates the first official kiosk to Kampala in 2013; The New Times says Jibu entered Rwanda in 2013; both fit 2013 pilots. Galen's 'proven model' and 'all three' quotations are from the SSIR transcript on the episode page. Aristotle's remark is about deliberation in general and is applied by analogy.
